Whosoever
hōo-sō-ev'er
pron. (universal relative; rendering Hebrew 'ish 'asher and kol constructions, Greek pas ho and hos an)
A compound of whoso and ever, strengthening the relative into a universal. It leaves the person unnamed and the class unbounded: whoever he may be, of whatever nation or condition, the sentence applies to him.

Biblical Definition

Whosoever is the universal relative, and it does two opposite kinds of work in Scripture with equal force. In the law it universalises the penalty: “Whosoever lieth with a beast shall surely be put to death” (Exodus 22:19), where no rank or circumstance exempts the offender. In the gospel it universalises the offer: “whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life” (John 3:16); “whosoever shall call upon the name of the Lord shall be saved” (Romans 10:13); “whosoever will, let him take the water of life freely” (Revelation 22:17). The word names no one and excludes no one. It does not teach that all will be saved, nor that men come to Christ of their own unaided will; it teaches that the invitation is addressed without qualification to every hearer, so that no sinner may plead that the gospel was not offered to him. The Reformed reading of these texts has always been this: the call goes out indiscriminately to all, and it is made effectual in the elect by the Spirit. Whosoever is the warrant on which any man may come.

Webster 1828 Definition

Whatever person; any one without exception. In Scripture it universalises both the sentence of the law, from which no offender is exempt, and the offer of the gospel, from which no hearer is excluded.

expand to see more

WHOSOEVER, pron. [who, so and ever.] Whatever person; any person whatever.

2. It is a compound relative, and includes both the antecedent and the relative; as, whosoever will, let him come.

3. It is emphatic, and excludes every exception of person, nation, rank or condition.

4. The corresponding forms are whatsoever of things, whomsoever in the objective, and wheresoever of place.

5. In Scripture, whosoever believeth in him should not perish, John 3; whosoever shall call upon the name of the Lord shall be saved, Rom. 10.

Key Scripture

Exodus 22:19 — "Whosoever lieth with a beast shall surely be put to death."

John 3:16 — "For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life."

Romans 10:13 — "For whosoever shall call upon the name of the Lord shall be saved."

Revelation 22:17 — "And the Spirit and the bride say, Come. And let him that heareth say, Come. And let him that is athirst come. And whosoever will, let him take the water of life freely."

Modern Corruption

Whosoever is pressed into two opposite errors: universalism, which reads the free offer as a promise that all shall in fact be saved, and a hyper-Calvinism which grows shy of preaching the offer freely at all. Scripture's own use rebukes both.

expand to see more

The universalist reading takes the breadth of the offer for the breadth of the outcome. But whosoever believeth is a conditional promise, and the same Gospel that says should not perish also says he that believeth not is condemned already. Scripture nowhere teaches that all people will eventually be saved; it teaches an eternal, conscious judgment for the unrepentant, and every text that widens the offer is set beside a text that narrows the number of those who take it. The free offer is not a prediction. It is a summons, and a summons implies the possibility of refusal and the guilt of refusing.

The opposite error is rarer but real. Where the doctrines of grace are held without warmth, some have grown reluctant to press the gospel indiscriminately, as though a free offer to all were inconsistent with a definite atonement for the elect. The Reformed confessions know no such inconsistency. The 1689 speaks of the gospel being freely offered to sinners, and the whole Puritan tradition preached it so — Bunyan on the jerusalem sinner, Flavel on the fountain opened. Christ's work is effectual for His people; the call is published to every creature; and it is precisely the whosoever that gives the awakened conscience its right to come. To mute it is to withhold the very warrant God has provided.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew builds the universal relative with kol (all, every) or with 'ish 'asher (the man who); Greek uses pas ho with a participle, or hos an with the subjunctive; English compounds who, so, and ever.

expand to see more

Hebrew kol (H3605) — all, every, the whole; the ordinary way of making a statute or promise universal.

Greek pas (G3956) — all, every; with the article and a participle it yields every one that believeth.

Greek hos an (G3739, G302) — whosoever; the relative with the particle of contingency, leaving the person indefinite.

Greek pisteuo (G4100) — to believe, to trust; the participle governed by whosoever in John 3:16.

Greek epikaleomai (G1941) — to call upon, to invoke; the verb of Romans 10:13 and of Acts 2:21.

Usage

"Of the law admitting no exemption: Whosoever lieth with a beast shall surely be put to death (Exodus 22:19)."

"Of the gospel offered without qualification: whosoever believeth in him should not perish (John 3:16)."

"Of the invitation closing the canon: whosoever will, let him take the water of life freely (Revelation 22:17)."
